summary: Describes an information model for Kerberos version 5 from the standpoint of an administrative service. Since there is no standard for administering a Key Distribution Center, it describes what services an administrative interface to one exposes.

eli5.summary: A list of the jobs the manager of a ticket office needs to do, such as adding people and fixing accounts, written so anyone can build a control panel.

questions: how to administer a kerberos kdc
what is the kerberos information model
how do you administer a kerberos kdc
subtitle: A neutral list of what a Kerberos ticket server stores, so that it can be administered the same way everywhere.

tldr.problem: RFC 4120 says how Kerberos authenticates but not how a Key Distribution Center (KDC) is managed, and several different "kadmin" servers grew up without a standard.
tldr.mechanism: It defines an abstract information model: principals, KeySets, Keys and Policies, each with named attributes and associations, which can be mapped onto LDAP, SQL, XML or other schemas.
tldr.outcome: The model is not a schema or a protocol itself. It is a common vocabulary that administrative interfaces can implement, and it requires that keys never travel in the clear.

today: RFC 6880 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is an abstract model rather than a wire protocol, so it describes what an administrative interface should expose, not how to talk to one.

sections.title: Why a Model for Administering Kerberos
sections.content:
The Kerberos version 5 authentication service (RFC 4120) describes how a Key Distribution Center (KDC) authenticates clients, but not how a KDC is managed. Several "kadmin" servers evolved on their own. This document describes the services needed to administer a KDC and the information model a kadmin-type service assumes.

The model uses "attributes" and "services" or "interfaces", but this implies no modeling paradigm. It is neither object-oriented nor an LDAP schema. An implementation MAY rename things (for example principalName) but MUST supply a name-to-name mapping and call out its naming conventions, and MUST support default attribute values and syntax for attribute values.
sections.eli5: Every ticket office had its own private way to be run. This RFC writes down the common jobs so offices can be managed the same way.

sections.title: How the Requirement Words Are Used
sections.content:
Because the model is mapped to a schema language rather than used directly, the RFC adjusts the RFC 2119 keywords. MUST means a schema has a way to represent the feature, though the schema may still treat it as optional, and also that a KDC or admin interface must provide the behavior. MUST NOT be OPTIONAL means the feature is mandatory and must be present in every representation of the object.

SHOULD and RECOMMENDED mean the consequences of departing from the rule must be weighed carefully, and that interoperability may suffer. Context decides whether a SHOULD applies to the schema, the KDC behavior, or both; for example, principalIsDisabled SHOULD default to FALSE, which is both a behavior and a schema recommendation.

The model is explicitly not a schema: how objects are compared for equality, and the ordering of elements, are not specified. It also notes that password-policy elements are not unique to Kerberos, so an LDAP mapping should reuse existing LDAP schema where it overlaps.
sections.eli5: The words MUST and SHOULD mean a bit more here, because the list will later be turned into a real database. MUST means the database has to be able to hold it.

sections.title: Principals
sections.content:
The principal is the fundamental entity in a KDC. It is associated with keys and generalizes the idea of a user. It MUST be implemented in full and MUST NOT be optional.

Its attributes include principalName (unique within the KDC's administrative context, equivalent to the string form of the name including the realm; it may be multivalued for aliases or enterprise names, with one canonical value), principalNotUsedBefore and principalNotUsedAfter (dates in RFC 3339 format), principalIsDisabled, and time stamps for creation, modification and last credential change.

It also has principalMaximumTicketLifetime and principalMaximumRenewableTicketLifetime, both in seconds, and an optional principalAllowedEnctype list; if that list is empty or absent, any encryption type the implementation supports is allowed. A principal may have zero or more KeySets and zero or more Policies.
sections.eli5: A principal is a name on the ticket office's list: a person or a service. Each name has a card with dates, an on/off switch, and how long its tickets may last.

sections.title: KeySets and Keys
sections.content:
Principals have zero or more secret keys, each with a key version number (kvno) and an encryption type (enctype). The model groups keys by kvno into KeySet objects. A principal may have several, which helps with key rollover, and implementations MUST NOT assume exactly one. Each KeySet has one or more keys and belongs to exactly one principal, and it MUST NOT hold two keys with the same enctype. The kvno is a non-negative integer incremented by one each time a key in the set changes.

A Key has a keyEncryptionType (the IANA string name, for example aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96), a keyValue and a keySaltValue (single-valued octet strings), a keyStringToKeyParameter (see RFC 3961), validity dates, and a keyIsDisabled flag that SHOULD default to FALSE. Implementations MUST NOT force keys to be represented, so a schema that required keys to be present would not conform. Where keys are implemented, they need adequate protection from unauthorized modification and disclosure.
sections.eli5: Each name can have secret keys in numbered batches. When a key is changed the batch number goes up by one, so old and new can overlap for a while.

sections.title: Policies
sections.content:
Implementations SHOULD implement policies but MAY make them optional. A policy is a "typed hole": an opaque binary value paired with an identifier of its type. Attributes are policyIdentifier (globally unique, for example an OID, a URI or a UUID), policyIsCritical (the KDC MUST understand and apply the policy for the principal to be used), an optional policyContent and an optional policyUse for initial filtering.

Implementations that represent policy objects MUST be able to represent four kinds: password quality (requirements on new passwords), password management (how passwords are changed), keying (which enctypes go to new principals), and ticket flag (which ticket flags are allowed). The RFC does not model a policy expression language, noting that expressing policy may in general require a Turing-complete language.
sections.eli5: Policies are the house rules, like how long a password must be. The model just says where to keep a rule without spelling out each one.

sections.title: Implementation Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC sketches four ways to build an administrative service from the model. With an LDAP backend, the KDC stores principals and keys in a directory server; non-key data is administered through the directory while keys change through the set/change password protocol. With an LDAP frontend, the KDC exposes its non-key objects as LDAP entries while keeping its native database.

An XML schema implementation could support a SOAP interface, and a YAML implementation could support a NETCONF interface for standard network management applications. These examples show the value of an abstract model that maps to several schema representations.
sections.eli5: Because the list is abstract, you can build the control panel in different ways, like a phone book program or a web service.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Kerberos depends on the security of the keys in the KDC. The model assumes keys MUST NOT travel in the clear and are write-only attributes, changed through the administrative interface only by the change-password protocol.

Exposing a KDC's objects usually means they can be modified or deleted, and not all principals are equal: deleting krbtgt/EXAMPLE.COM@EXAMPLE.COM effectively disables the EXAMPLE.COM realm. Access control is therefore paramount, but this document does not mandate it, so it may not be reachable via any protocol based on the model. Exposing access control objects could itself reveal which principals have elevated rights.
sections.eli5: The secret keys must never be shouted across the room, and only a few people should be allowed to change the list, because erasing one special name can shut the whole office.
